doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Benny Golson's New York Scene and Paul Chambers lying down during Whisper Not
summary: Golson explains the larger ensemble writing, arrangements by Ernie Wilkins and Gigi Gryce, and a tipsy Paul Chambers stopping and lying down on the last tune.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Then again in that year, ’57 – and these are all from the fall or early winter. I’m trying to get the chronology here. Here’s one from October. This one that I just mentioned, The Modern Touch, was from December. Here in October ’57, also on Riverside, was Benny Golson’s New York Scene. Here it looks like you’ve already got a precursor of what – of things to come. First of all, this one has – it’s got several cuts that have an expanded orchestra. You’ve got Julius Watkins on french horn. You’ve got Sahib Shihab. So, a larger ensemble – that seems to be something that you’ve favored throughout your career, writing for larger ensemble? You’re versatile, writing for a variety of formats. Any recollections about this particular album?

Yeah. You speak about a format. That was so, because it permitted me to write, to explore the writing possibilities as well as the playing. That was my very first one as a leader. What was it? New York Scene?
Yes. Benny Golson’s New York Scene.

On it, Ernie Wilkins wrote a couple of arrangements. I didn’t want to have just me, somehow. I think he wrote a couple of arrangements. I’m not sure – yeah, Gigi Gryce. I think he wrote one or two. Then I wrote the rest. I think we did a couple of quintet things too.
Yeah. They’re doubled up. You got Art Farmer on there, Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers, Charlie Persip.

Yeah, Paul Chambers. We got to the last tune of the session, which was Whisper Not. They usually bring in sandwiches and some alcohol – beer and stuff. Paul had a little too much. We got to this last tune. We started recording it, and he stopped playing, right in the middle. When I turned around and looked, he was looking at the music like, “What the heck is this?” I said, oh my goodness. “Let’s start over again.” We started over again, and he stopped again. He was looking at it like he didn’t understand what – I could see he had had too much. He’d been under the influence. I begged him. I said, “Paul, please, please. This is my” – we tried it again. He stopped again. Then he put his bass down. He was on a little riser. He laid down, like he was through for the day. I said, “Paul, please, please, get up. Please, Paul. This is my first record date.” Then he got up, and he made it. That was Whisper Not.
